job.style: a passage rich in numbers, dates or measurements

response.passage: Rohan needs a loan of Rs 1,00,000 for his small business. Bank A offers a simple interest loan at 10% per annum for 2 years, meaning he pays Rs 20,000 as interest plus the principal. Bank B offers a compound interest loan at 10% per annum, compounded annually. Rohan must understand that for the first year, both simple and compound interest yield the same Rs 10,000 charge. However, in the second year, compound interest applies to the new total, making it costlier. Rohan also considers a credit card for emergency supplies. He learns that the interest-free period only applies if he pays his entire outstanding balance in full by the due date. If he pays only a partial amount, the bank charges interest on the full balance from the purchase date. Furthermore, he compares two loan schemes: a flat rate of 8% and a reducing-balance rate of 8%. He discovers the reducing-balance method is cheaper because interest is calculated only on the remaining unpaid principal each month, whereas the flat rate charges interest on the original loan amount throughout the tenure. Finally, he notes that a 6-month loan requires setting the time variable T to 0.5 years in the interest formula, as rates are quoted per annum.
response.summary: This passage explains the differences between simple and compound interest, the mechanics of credit card debt, and how loan calculation methods like reducing-balance affect total costs. It clarifies that interest rates are annual and time must be adjusted accordingly for shorter periods.
